entries.title: Congo, M23 rebels agree to peace roadmap
entries.summary: Negotiators representing the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda-backed M23 rebels have agreed to a roadmap for peace. The US State Department, a mediator, released a joint statement.
entries.content:
Democratic Republic of Congo

Congo, M23 rebels agree to peace roadmap

August 23, 2026

Negotiators representing the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda-backed M23 rebels have agreed to a roadmap for peace. The US State Department, a mediator, released a joint statement.

After days of negotiations in Geneva, Switzerland, representatives from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) and the Rwanda-backed rebel group M23 have agreed to a shared roadmap designed to facilitate peace in the DRC after years of brutal war. 

The US State Department, which was involved in mediating talks alongside the African Union (AU), Switzerland and Qatar, released a statement describing the situation on Saturday evening.

The State Department said the agreement builds on a US-brokered deal signed last November in Doha, Qatar, adding that Congo and the rebels had "developed a roadmap setting out sequenced steps and timelines for negotiations under the Doha Framework Agreement."

Despite a ceasefire being in place since November 15, the shift to peace has been slow, though prisoners, for instance, were recently exchanged.

The newly agreed roadmap made clear that an observer mission monitoring the ceasefire will receive support from UN MONUSCO peacekeeping forces and that further negotiations designed to bring about lasting peace will take place soon.

Hundreds of civilians have been killed and millions displaced by fighting between the two sides since early 2022, when M23 — with backing from neighboring Rwanda — began its quest for control of resource-rich eastern Congo and its gold, cassiterite, coltan and diamonds.

M23, which is accused of committing brutal wartime atrocities, has controlled large swaths of the North and South Kivu provinces since 2025.

The State Department statement released on Saturday said both sides had thanked mediators "for their steadfast support in advancing peace and stability in eastern DRC and the broader Great Lakes region."

entries.title: Harry Kane named footballer of the year in Germany
entries.summary: Harry Kane has added another honor after a remarkable season for Bayern Munich and a strong World Cup with England. Bayern also took the top prize in coaching, and the club's Giulia Gwinn won women's Player of the Year.
entries.content:
August 23, 2026

Harry Kane has added another honor after a remarkable season for Bayern Munich and a strong World Cup with England. Bayern also took the top prize in coaching, and the club's Giulia Gwinn won women's Player of the Year.

Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane has been named men's Player of the Year in Germany after a record-breaking season for the Bundesliga champions.

Bayern coach Vincent Kompany was voted trainer of the year, while Germany defender Giulia Gwinn completed a clean sweep for the Munich club by winning the women's Player of the Year award.

"A Bayern double — never before have the men and women's Player of the Year awards gone to the same club. Congratulations to Harry and Giulia, as well as our coach Vincent," Bayern president Herbert Hainer said in a club statement. "When men's and women's football makes history together, then that's Bayern, making a mark. We're proud of this result."

Why was Harry Kane named Germany's footballer of the year?

Kane received 272 votes from members of the Association of German Sports Journalists, comfortably ahead of Bayern teammate Michael Olise on 203.

Stuttgart and Germany striker Deniz Undav finished third with 61 votes.

England captain Kane scored 61 goals in 51 competitive appearances for Bayern last season.

"It was the best season of my career so far," Kane said last week after winning the European Golden Shoe for the second time.

His club form was followed by another strong World Cup run with England, where he scored six goals as the team reached the semifinals. Kane also became England's all-time leading scorer at World Cups, taking his overall tournament tally to 14.

The 33-year-old was also awarded the European Golden Shoe for the second time in his career after finishing as the continent's leading league goalscorer.

Former Bayern striker Luca Toni said Kane also deserved to win the Ballon d'Or, football's leading individual award.

Kompany takes coach of the year, Gwinn wins women's award

Kompany was the clear winner among coaches, receiving 314 votes after guiding Bayern to a league and cup double.

Freiburg coach Julian Schuster, who won the award last year, finished second with 87 votes, while Stuttgart's Sebastian Hoeneß was third with 53.

Schuster praised Kompany's work, saying the Belgian was not only a good coach but also made those around him better.

Gwinn won the women's award outright after sharing first place with goalkeeper Ann-Katrin Berger last year.

"This is an honor and a validation of my journey," Gwinn said.

The 27-year-old Bayern defender received 106 votes, narrowly beating teammate Klara Bühl on 94.

entries.title: Ukraine: Zelenskyy rejects wartime elections
entries.summary: The Ukrainian president says wartime elections, as called for by the ex-defense minister, could "split Ukraine." He also said Russia was planning to mobilize hundreds of thousands of troops after September polls there.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine: Zelenskyy rejects wartime elections

August 23, 2026

The Ukrainian president says wartime elections, as called for by the ex-defense minister, could "split Ukraine." He also said Russia was planning to mobilize hundreds of thousands of troops after September polls there.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that holding elections in his country amid the full-scale Russian invasion would be highly dangerous, in remarks made in response to a call from the former defense minister to organize a vote.

"I believe that in a war like this, elections as such are a huge risk. Elections right now are a tsunami for the country that will split Ukraine," Zelenskyy said in remarks released on Sunday.

Under martial law, elections are currently suspended in the country as it fights the invading Russian forces. The measure has wide public support.

What did Zelenskyy say about the proposed election?

"If we want to destroy the country, then we can move in the direction of elections during these times of war," Zelenskyy said in the firm rejection of the proposal by former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov.

Fedorov made the call a month after being fired by Zelenskyy as defense minister.

Fedorov enjoys significant support among younger Ukrainians, thousands of whom have been calling for his reinstatement, with some saying he could seek to challenge Zelenskyy if an election did take place.

However, a recent poll showed that Zelenskyy would still be more popular as a presidential candidate.

Zelenskyy was critical of Fedorov in his remarks, saying: "I believe he is going himself — or is being pushed — toward wrong things."

Russia planning mass mobilization — Zelenskyy

Zelenskyy also said that Kyiv believed Russia was planning to mobilize 300,000 more troops for its invasion after parliamentary elections take place in September.

He added that Moscow might draft hundreds of thousands more in 2027 as it seeks to capture the rest of Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region, one of its main strategic goals.

Agreement on missile interceptors from Germany

As Ukraine continues to come under intense missile attacks from its neighbor, Zelenskyy also spoke of having struck an agreement with Germany on the supply of 600 Patriot PAC-2 missile interceptors for 2027-28.

The announcement comes after German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul visited Ukraine on Saturday.

The US Patriots are the only weapon in Kyiv's arsenal that can take on Russia's Iskander-M and Kinzhal ballistic missiles, but ammunition for the system is running short.

France on Saturday also promised to deliver new interceptor missiles.

As Europe seeks to fill the gap left by a US that, under Donald Trump, has shown ever more reluctance to help Ukraine, Norway has also said it plans to ‌give ⁠another ⁠85 billion Norwegian ​crowns ($9.2 billion; €7.8 billion) in ​financial ​support ‌to Kyiv in the 2027 ‌fiscal year.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Is the US seeing a turning point in obesity rates?
entries.summary: Obesity rates climbed in the US for years, but now there are signs this could be changing. Use of weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic and Wegovy has increased rapidly — are they helping?
entries.content:
August 23, 2026

Obesity rates climbed in the US for years, but now there are signs this could be changing. Use of weight-loss drugs such as Ozempic and Wegovy has increased rapidly — are they helping?

The United States has been grappling with an obesity epidemic since the late 1970s, but there is growing evidence that the constantly climbing obesity rates are beginning to drop.

"We're seeing signs that there's going to be a turning point," said Benjamin Rader, an epidemiologist at Boston Children's Hospital and at Harvard Medical School who conducts research into health trends using large datasets. In 2024, he and his colleagues published a study based on data from more than 16 million adults, which suggested there had been a decline in obesity prevalence in 2023 — for the first time in more than 10 years.

The National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey also indicated a slight decline between 2021 and 2023. More recent surveys have also provided evidence of declining figures.

Use of Ozempic, Wegovy and Zepbound skyrockets

This comes as a series of new drugs, which some people are using for weight loss, have come onto the market. The use of the GLP-1 agonist drugs Ozempic, Wegovy and Zepbound has increased rapidly in recent years in the US, with prescriptions more than quadrupling between 2021 and early 2026.

Some of the active ingredients in these drugs were originally developed to treat Type 2 diabetes by mimicking a naturally occurring intestinal hormone to promote a feeling of fullness and to slow down gastric emptying. This has led to many patients losing a significant amount of weight.

For Rader, "it seemed like it [the impact of this medicine] was bound to show up in the data" and that it was possible to be "moderately confident that drugs themselves were having an effect."

'Strong evidence showing significant decline in obesity'

For Peminda Cabandugama, an endocrinologist and spokesperson for The Obesity Society, which provides support to professionals in the obesity field, "there is strong evidence showing that there is a significant decline in obesity."

In a written statement to DW, he said the "general opinion is that GLP-1 medications and their combinations and their increased use as well as the recent attention put on the importance of weight management have played a large and direct role in this reduction in obesity prevalence."

But for Rader there is no definitive proof of a causal relationship. He has no doubt that the drugs have led to weight loss in many people at an individual level, but he told DW that it was too soon to say whether it "will lead to a plateau, […] a decrease […] or a slower decrease in the next 20 years" and what the effect on the general population might be.

Cabandugama thinks the current figures might also have been influenced by lifestyle changes during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, and points out that "these trends are likely a confluence of multiple elements that include the increased use of anti-obesity medications, post-pandemic behavioral changes, increased awareness about the importance of weight management etc."

Is the decline temporary?

Some researchers in the US don't believe obesity rates will decline permanently. A study by the Institute of Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) at the University of Washington in Seattle predicts a rise in rates through 2035 and suggests that the proportion of obese adults could increase from 42.5% in 2022 to 46.9% in 2035.

Though Rader doesn't necessarily consider such predictions to be wrong, he pointed out that many prediction models are based on data from before the boom in GLP-1 drugs and might not take into account their potential effects. In an article for the Journal of the American Medical Association, he warned that the models could overestimate the future burden of obesity.

The authors of the IHME study have not entirely dismissed this criticism, but they did point out that to date only a small proportion of obese people use such drugs and that many patients discontinue treatment within a year. They added that some people gain weight again after initially losing it, and more representative data was needed to assess whether such drugs will have a lasting effect on obesity rates.

Cabandugama has also urged caution, saying that while there are currently strong signs of a decline, "the general consensus is that it is still too early to tell whether this is a true trend reversal."

Consequences of decline in obesity rates would be far-reaching

Though for a long time, obesity was viewed primarily as a result of an individual's lifestyle, it has since become well-known that this complex chronic condition is caused by a combination of biological, genetic, social and psychological factors.

If the US were at a turning point, the consequences would be far-reaching. Weight loss in obese people does not only reduce their risk of related health problems, but also contributes to greater mobility, more independence and a higher quality of life.

For Cabandugama, "the health outcomes to improve first would be betterments in cardiometabolic parameters: blood glucose levels (Type 2 diabetes mellitus), cardiovascular outcomes, fatty liver, obstructive sleep apnea etc.," which in the long term could also reduce pressure on the healthcare system.

Regardless of whether rates are on the decline, Rader said "obesity still remains a huge public health crisis in America that deserves attention, deserves funding, and deserves alternative solutions, especially as we think about how GLP-1s are not accessible to all Americans based on price and other factors."

"A turning point does not mean that we're suddenly in the clear and that we don't have to worry about this thing anymore," he said.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: What is the 'political firewall' against Germany's far-right AfD?
entries.summary: Germany's centrist parties reject any cooperation with the Alternative for Germany (AfD), parts of which are classified as right-wing extremist. However, this policy is coming under increasing pressure.
entries.content:
Germany

What is the 'political firewall' against Germany's AfD?

August 23, 2026

Germany's centrist parties reject any cooperation with the Alternative for Germany (AfD), parts of which are classified as right-wing extremist. However, this policy is coming under increasing pressure.

A firewall is a wall designed to prevent a fire from spreading from one building to another. In German politics, the term "firewall" serves as a metaphor for a strict boundary drawn against parties regarded as extremist. Just as a firewall is intended to protect buildings from fire, the "political firewall" is intended to safeguard democracy.

Whether the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is in fact a party that is hostile to democracy has not yet been determined by the courts. While Germany's domestic intelligence agency, the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, has classified individual AfD state associations as "confirmed right-wing extremist," the question of whether the party as a whole is acting against the German constitution would have to be decided by the Federal Constitutional Court in proceedings to ban the party.

Calls for an AfD ban have been made repeatedly, but no formal application has been filed to date.

Chancellor Merz is growing tired of the term 'firewall'

The term "political firewall" cannot be clearly attributed to any single originator. However, its widespread use is due in large part to Friedrich Merz.

Upon becoming leader of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in December 2021, for example, he told the German news magazine Der Spiegel: "Under my leadership, there will be a firewall against the AfD."

In 2018, the CDU adopted a so-called "resolution of incompatibility" at its party conference, rejecting "coalitions and similar forms of cooperation" with both the AfD and the socialist Left Party.

This did not apply only to formal agreements and coalitions with the AfD. At times, the CDU also deliberately sought majorities without AfD support, and CDU officeholders declined to be elected to political positions with AfD votes.

January 2025 marked a break from that path: A CDU motion in the Bundestag calling for the rejection of asylum seekers passed with AfD support. At the time, Merz was leader of the CDU and thus of the parliamentary opposition. To this day, critics continue to accuse him of breaching the firewall policy.

Now chancellor, Merz tends to avoid the term and has grown increasingly irritated by questions about it.

The center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the ecologist Greens reject any cooperation with the AfD, although without formal resolutions to that effect. Sahra Wagenknecht, founder of the left-wing populist Alliance Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW), takes a different stance. She explicitly opposes excluding the AfD and would even be willing to pave the way for an AfD-led government in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, where elections will be held on September 6.



No firewall at the municipal level

The reliance on AfD votes by Merz's CDU in January 2025 triggered shock and outrage, but it wasn't the first time a politician who officially supports the firewall doesn't adhere to it in practice. In 2020, Thomas Kemmerich from the neoliberal FDP was elected Premier of Thuringia with AfD votes.

Angela Merkel, who was chancellor at the time, was alarmed and demanded that the election "must be reversed."

Kemmerich resigned just a few days later.

At the local level, however, the firewall is often highly permeable. In city and municipal councils, politicians from other parties have repeatedly voted alongside the AfD. Proponents of this more relaxed attitude often argue that, for example, building a daycare center does not become a bad idea simply because the AfD also supports it.

Critics, however, regularly warn of a gradual process of normalization. In their view, such cooperation makes the AfD socially acceptable, and what begins in local politics could eventually spread to state or even federal politics.

Can 40% of voters be ignored?

The firewall policy does not appear to be harming the AfD. On the contrary, its poll ratings continue to rise, despite, or perhaps even because of, the firewall.

When the AfD is particularly strong, as it is across much of eastern Germany, the other parties represented in state parliaments often have to join forces to prevent an AfD-led state government. This can come at the expense of the credibility of parties whose ideological positions are far apart.

Political scientists also point to a democratic deficit if the political preferences of AfD voters are ignored over the long term.

Sahra Wagenknecht (BSW) recently said of Saxony-Anhalt: "It is simply completely undemocratic to permanently exclude a party supported by around 40% of voters. The firewall has failed."

Some CDU politicians in eastern Germany have questioned the rationale behind the firewall. The Brandenburg branch of the Small and Medium Enterprises and Economic Union, an internal CDU interest group, recently submitted a motion calling on the party "at the federal level to work toward repealing or fundamentally revising the CDU's incompatibility resolution vis-a-vis the AfD."

Following strong criticism from the federal party leadership, the group withdrew the motion.

Saxony's CDU Premier Michael Kretschmer, who leads a minority government in Dresden, recently told the German business daily Handelsblatt: "Anyone still talking about firewalls has failed to recognize the signs of the times. We need to talk to everyone who is willing to talk."

At the federal level, the CDU would prefer to put an end to such debates altogether. Thorsten Frei, the new chair of the Bundestag's conservative parliamentary group, which includes the Christian Social Union (CSU), has made clear that he will not tolerate deviations by individual state branches. 

"The ban on cooperation with the AfD is a fundamental party resolution of the CDU. It cannot be interpreted differently from one federal state to another," he told newspapers belonging to the Funke Media Group.

The chancellor, too, is holding firm now. Despite the immense pressure and the challenging political landscape in eastern Germany, and aside from the break in January 2025, he continues to uphold the resolution of incompatibility with both the AfD and the Left Party.

How governing majorities opposed to the AfD can be formed in the future therefore remains an open question.

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Kazakhstan parliamentary vote to cement president's power
entries.summary: Candidates from seven state-approved parties are taking part in the election, while opposition parties have been banned. Central Asia's largest nation, Kazakhstan maintains a delicate balance between Russia and the West.
entries.content:
Kazakhstan

Kazakhstan parliamentary vote to cement president's power

August 23, 2026

Candidates from seven state-approved parties are taking part in the election, while opposition parties have been banned. Central Asia's largest nation, Kazakhstan maintains a delicate balance between Russia and the West.

Kazakhstan's 12.3 million eligible voters will elect the Central Asian country's parliament on Sunday.

The polls come after a new constitution approved in March did away with the Senate to create a new unicameral Kurultai — a reference to the medieval councils of the region's nomadic past.

Backers of the new body say it will give parliament more say in decision making, critics argue it will only cement the power of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.

The 73-year-old took the reins from authoritarian Nursultan Nazarbayev — who himself ruled the country for 30 years after the collapse of the Soviet Union — in 2019.

The pro-presidential Adilet party is expected to win an overwhelming majority in Sunday's vote, with a number of smaller parties loyal to Tokayev also pegged to enter parliament.

Seven state-approved parties have been allowed to field candidates for the 145-seat parliament while genuine opposition parties have been banned.

The election is taking place amid soaring inflation (which is hovering around 10.2%) and rising taxes, fueling concerns for the government — and particularly Tokayev — of a repeat of January 2022 cost of living unrest that left 238 protesters and police dead.

Press crackdown and financial strain color Kazakhstan's election

Beyond financial strain, Sunday's vote is also taking place against the background of crackdowns on press freedom, with numerous reporters under house arrest and official criminal cases being brought against 10 independent journalists and bloggers.

Tokayev, a former Soviet official and Kazakh diplomat who worked at the UN, has touted his reforms and justified the many changes he has initiated — including the introduction of the new constitution — as necessary in a fast-changing world.

"Without a doubt, these elections will be remembered as perhaps the most interesting in our country's history," said Tokayev on Friday.

"Amid unprecedented geopolitical tensions and mounting global challenges, we must firmly and consistently implement our strategy to transform Kazakhstan into a truly developed state," he added.

Tokayev has sought to maintain a delicate balance between Moscow — with their shared Soviet ties — and the West since sanctions were imposed on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine. Resource-rich and strategically located Kazakhstan also has ties to China and the European Union.

Although Tokayev has said that he has no plans of staying in power beyond his current term, the constitutional reform that 87% of voters backed this March effectively reset term limits for the office — making him eligible to run for another seven-year stint in 2029 should he change his mind.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Search resumes for 22 crew after cargo ship sinks off India
entries.summary: The Panama‑flagged Ocean Winner had 24 people on board when it sank in the Bay of Bengal. The ship is thought to have been carrying iron ore from India to Singapore.
entries.content:
Published August 22, 2026last updated August 23, 2026

The Panama‑flagged Ocean Winner had 24 people on board when it sank in the Bay of Bengal. The ship is thought to have been carrying iron ore from India to Singapore.

A search-and-rescue operation was continuing on Sunday after a cargo ship sank off the eastern coast of India.

The Panama-flagged vessel Ocean Winner had 24 crew on board when it sank on Friday. Two Chinese nationals were rescued on Saturday, with 22 people still unaccounted for, the Indian Coast Guard said.

The two rescued Chinese seafarers said the vessel developed a list on Friday and ​sank within eight minutes, forcing crew to abandon ship, said Shyam Jagannathan, ​director general of India's Maritime Administration.

'Developing a list' is a technical maritime term which means the vessel began tilting. The cause for this was not immediately known.

Search on for missing crew members

The chances of finding survivors fell sharply after 12 hours, but rescuers were continuing the search, Jagannathan ​said.

The missing crew members include 18 ‌Chinese ​nationals, three Myanmar nationals

and one Bangladeshi, according to the Indian Coast Guard. In a post on X, it said it had deployed three ships to conduct surface searches for the remaining crew members.

According to officials cited in the Indian Express, the ship was about 240 nautical miles (444 kilometers, 276 miles) off the coast of Odisha.

According to ship-tracking app MarineTraffic, the Ocean Winner was carrying iron ore from Paradip port in Odisha to Singapore.

entries.title: Trump hits out at Canada over retaliatory tariffs
entries.summary: Donald Trump has accused Canada of treating US farmers unfairly for years as a trade standoff between Ottawa and Washington escalates. Both sides are threatening new tariffs after the collapse of talks on Friday.
entries.content:
August 23, 2026

Donald Trump has accused Canada of treating US farmers unfairly for years as a trade standoff between Ottawa and Washington escalates. Both sides are threatening new tariffs after the collapse of talks on Friday.

US President Donald Trump on Sunday accused Canada of wanting "the benefits of being a [US] State, without being one" in his first remarks since trade talks between Ottawa and Washington failed.

"They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of Tariffs. No more!!!" he wrote on his social media platform Truth Social.

What has happened in the US-Canada trade dispute?

In an ongoing trade dispute with the United States, Canada said on Saturday that it would introduce tariffs on several US products starting September 8.

The announcement comes in retaliation to the US imposing 50% tariffs earlier on Saturday on a broad range of Canadian products after the two sides failed to reach a trade deal on Friday.

"Canada will match Washington's new ⁠tariffs ​dollar for dollar in order to protect ​Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses," Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters in Ottawa.

"In the coming days, we will release the details of these new tariff measures, which will come into force the Tuesday after Labor Day," he said.

While the US had blamed Canada for declining to finalize the trade pact with Washington on Friday, Carney defended Ottawa's position, explaining, "We cannot accept what they have offered, and we will not give what they have asked."

He later on Saturday met virtually with provincial and territorial premiers to discuss the suspension of the trade talks with the US.

What products are affected by the tariffs?

The US tariffs will affect a broad range of products, including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing ‌rods, and hockey ​equipment, and cover some $20 billion (€17 billion) worth of Canadian exports to its southern neighbor.

Canada's retaliatory tariffs would, in turn, target steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics, Carney said.

The US currently accounts for roughly 70% of Canadian exports, making Ottawa potentially more vulnerable in the standoff Carney explicitly described as a trade "war."

"You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked," he said, adding that Canada had the reserves, resilience and plan to respond.

How have Canadian and US politicians reacted?

Doug Ford, the premier of Canada's most populous province Ontario and one of the most vocal opponents of US President Donald Trump's tariffs, slammed the proposed trade deal and backed Carney's decision to retaliate.

"I'm glad he didn't sign that deal because it was a bad deal. It was a bad deal for Ontario. It was a bad deal for the auto sector, the steel sector and ​manufacturing sector," Ford said on Saturday.

Meanwhile, Pierre Poilievre, the leader of the official opposition Conservative Party, urged Canadians to "stand united to defend our country against these unfair attacks on our jobs and businesses."

In the US, Democratic lawmakers and governors have blamed Trump for the escalating trade conflict.

"Needlessly picking fights with our allies and raising prices here at home. That's Trump's economic policy in a nutshell," New York Governor Kathy Hochul posted on X.

Michigan Congresswoman Haley Stevens also slammed "Trump's reckless and unnecessary trade war."

Friendly ties turned sour

The fresh tariffs are the culmination of long and tense trade negotiations between the two sides and mark a sharp reversal from just two days earlier, when officials from Washington and Ottawa appeared optimistic that a compromise was in the making.

According to the AP news agency, no further talks were planned to resolve the situation.

The US administration's approach to Canada is a major change from the friendly ties the two countries have traditionally had.

Trump has often said he wants tariffs on Canadian goods to encourage companies to move manufacturing back to the US.

He has also made controversial comments about making Canada the 51st US state. Carney said Canada understood that "America has changed" and that the two countries would "not return to their old relationship."

Edited by: Sean Sinico and Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Australia confirms H5N1 bird flu case in local mammal
entries.summary: Australian authorities said the deadly virus's spread to mammals was "concerning" but "not unexpected."
entries.content:
August 23, 2026

Australian authorities said the deadly virus's spread to mammals was "concerning" but "not unexpected."

Australia confirmed its first case of H5N1 bird flu in a mammal on Sunday, after it found the deadly virus in a long-nosed fur seal.

Authorities in the state of South Australia said they found the virus in the seal in the coastal town of Beachport, about 310 kilometers (192 miles) from the state capital, Adelaide.

Austrialia has been combating the highly pathogenic influenza after it arrived in the country in June. Earlier this month it reported its first mass seabird deaths, marking an escalation. 

What did authorities have to say?

There are an estimated 100,000 long-nosed fur seals in the state's waters. The infected individual was found dead with no signs of injury, authorities said.

Its death "does not ‌appear to be associated with other sick or dead ‌marine mammals," Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said in televised remarks.

"Once the H5 bird flu is spreading in the natural environment it is not possible to avoid significant losses," Collins added.

"Although this is a concerning development, it is not unexpected for us to start to see infection in other wildlife, particularly in marine mammals, particularly in areas where there are high infection rates in wild birds," Collins was quoted by the Australian Broadcasting Corporation as saying.

The virus has not spread to Australia's poultry or agriculture, according to the government, which counted 297 confirmed cases as of Friday.

Earlier in August, the government said it would begin a bird vaccination program based on the species' vulnerability to the virus and conservation impact.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

entries.title: Red faces as Sydney Marathon medal shows German stadium
entries.summary: A medal minted for finishers in the Sydney Marathon features a skyline of the city — with one landmark from rather far away. Organizers say the muddle only makes the medal "a little more unique."
entries.content:
August 23, 2026

A medal minted for finishers in the Sydney Marathon features a skyline of the city — with one landmark from rather far away. Organizers say the muddle only makes the medal "a little more unique."

Organizers of the 2026 Sydney Marathon are making the best of the situation after minting tens of thousands of medals engraved with depictions of landmarks from the eastern Australian city along with one that doesn't belong — the Allianz Arena in Munich, Germany.

The medal should have instead shown the Allianz Stadium in Sydney, which is one of the sights that participants in the upcoming race will pass while running the the 42.2-kilometer (26.2-mile) course.

More than 40,000 participants are expected to earn the medal as a "badge of honor" for completing the race on August 30.

Other landmarks shown include the famous Opera House and the Sydney Harbour Bridge.

What have organizers said about the medal mix-up?

"A little too much international flavor has found its way onto the back of the finishers medal, with an incorrect depiction of the stadium," a Sydney Marathon spokesperson said.

"We're not going to run from it, it was an unfortunate error; though it's certainly given everyone somehing to talk about this weekend, mostly in good humor," the spokesperson said.

"With the event a week away, this is the medal our finishers will receive."

"Behind every one of these medals is months of early mornings, long runs and quiet determination, and having it placed around your neck at the Sydney Opera House is a moment our participants will never forget," the spokesperson added.

"It's a beautiful medal, and now a little more unique."

Good-humored reaction from Munich

Munich's Allianz Arena has responded in light-hearted manner.

"Oh wow, we didn't have that on our bingo card!" it posted on Instagram.

"Perhaps they tried to find something else they had in common: Allianz Arena — Sydney Opera — Unique Architecture — Both are worth a visit!"

The daily Sydney Morning Herald also came up with a gleefully teasing headline: "The medal that will put Sydney on the map. The wrong map."

The other side of the medal shows shows a gold-and-indigo pattern by First Nations artist Ambrose Killian that has been widely commended.

Killian has said he was not involved in the design of the side showing the landmarks.
